    Biol Psychiatry. 2015 Oct 15;78(8):522-4. doi: 
10.1016/j.biopsych.2015.08.010.

BACKGROUND: Excessive anticipatory reactions to potential future adversity are 
observed across a range of anxiety disorders, but the neurogenetic mechanisms 
driving interindividual differences are largely unknown. We aimed to discover 
and validate a gene-brain-behavior pathway by linking presumed genetic risk for 
anxiety-related psychopathology, key neural activity involved in anxious 
anticipation, and resulting aversive emotional states.
METHODS: The functional neuroanatomy of aversive anticipation was probed through 
functional magnetic resonance imaging in two independent samples of healthy 
subjects (n = 99 and n = 69), and we studied the influence of genetic variance 
in the serotonin transporter linked polymorphic region (5-HTTLPR). Skin 
conductance and startle data served as objective psychophysiological indices of 
the intensity of individuals' anticipatory responses to potential threat.
RESULTS: Threat cues signaling risk of future electrical shock activated the 
dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC), anterior insula, bed nucleus of the stria 
terminalis, thalamus, and midbrain consistently across both samples. 
Threat-related dmPFC activation was enhanced in 5-HTTLPR short allele carriers 
in sample 1 and this effect was validated in sample 2. Critically, we show that 
this region mediates the increase in anticipatory psychophysiological reactions 
in short allele carriers indexed by skin conductance (experiment 1) and startle 
reactions (experiment 2).
CONCLUSIONS: The converging results from these experiments demonstrate that 
innate 5-HTTLPR linked variation in dmPFC activity predicts psychophysiological 
responsivity to pending threats. Our results reveal a neurogenetic pathway 
mediating interindividual variability in anticipatory responses to threat and 
yield a novel mechanistic account for previously reported associations between 
genetic variability in serotonin transporter function and stress-related 
psychopathology.

Previous research identified age-related changes in the parametric modulation of 
neural activity by emotional memory vividness. Within the dorsomedial prefrontal 
cortex (PFC), older adults showed a stronger relationship between neural 
recruitment and positive memory vividness, whereas younger adults showed a 
stronger relationship for negative memories. More work is needed to corroborate 
these Age × Valence interactions while clarifying if they are uniquely sensitive 
to vividness ratings made after an instructed elaboration period or predictive 
of how vividness ratings might change from initial recognition to 
postelaboration. The present study assessed a new sample of participants (n = 
60, ages 18-87) who completed a nearly identical paradigm as in previous work. 
Participants encoded emotional images paired with neutral titles and, during 
scanned retrieval, were presented with only the neutral titles in an old/new 
recognition task. Remembered titles were rated on the initial vividness of 
recollection for the paired image and a second rating of vividness after 
instructed elaboration. Results confirmed prefrontally mediated alterations to 
emotional memory phenomenology across the adult lifespan, evidenced by 
age-related increases in the relationship between PFC activity and positive 
memory vividness. During initial memory recognition, greater dorsomedial PFC 
activity among older adults predicted a subsequent increase in positive memory 
vividness after elaboration. Opposite patterns emerged in posterior sensorimotor 
and occipital regions that deactivated more strongly for vivid positive memories 
among older adults. These findings corroborate prior evidence of Age × Valence 
interactions in parametric modulation by vividness while also providing new 
evidence for a preparatory role of the PFC in shaping elaboration outcomes.

Low-grade inflammation in obesity causes low-effort food choice.

Scholing JM(1), Stienstra R(2), Olsthoorn L(1), Hendriksz MS(3), Mulders-Manders 
CM(3), van den Bosch R(1), Aarts E(4).

Author information:

(4)Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University, 
Nijmegen, The Netherlands. Electronic address: judith.scholing@donders.ru.nl.

Inflammation is related to decreased effortful behaviour and altered 
effort-related responses in several brain regions, such as the dorsomedial 
prefrontal cortex (dmPFC). While inflammation is prevalent in obesity, its 
effects on effortful versus more convenient food choices are currently unknown. 
We investigated the role of low-grade inflammation in effortful food choice 
behaviour using functional MRI in a cross-sectional study (n = 131 women, 
BMI > 27 kg/m2) and a 12-week randomized controlled trial investigating the 
effect of colchicine 0.5 mg/d vs. placebo (n = 49 women, BMI > 30 kg/m2, 
C-reactive protein (CRP) > 3 mg/l). Effort aversion was measured using a 
food-related effort-based decision-making task in which participants accepted or 
rejected offers to exert effort for food rewards. Inflammation (i.e. 
INFLA-score, a composite score of CRP, white blood cell count, 
neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, and platelets) was related to more effort 
aversion (i.e. a steeper decline in acceptance with increasing effort: 
OR = 0.27, p = 0.004) and higher effort-related dmPFC signal (β = 0.23, 
p = 0.025, Rpartial2 = 0.039). Furthermore, inflammation mediated the 
association between BMI and dmPFC signal. Colchicine treatment decreased 
systemic inflammation (INFLA-score: β = -0.40 SD, p < 0.001, Rpartial2 = 0.030), 
increased high-effort choices (OR = 1.32, p = 0.044), and marginally decreased 
effort-related dmPFC signal (β = -0.51, p = 0.053, Rpartial2 = 0.037) compared 
to placebo. These findings show a causal role for inflammation in choosing 
convenience foods in obesity via increased effort aversion and associated dmPFC 
processing.

Fairness decision-making in younger and older adults and associated neural 
indices.

Cho I(1), Barber N(2), Soo Goh JO(3)(4), Gutchess A(2).

Author information:
(1)Department of Psychology, Sungkyunkwan University, Seoul, Republic of Korea.
(2)Department of Psychology, Brandeis University, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA.
(3)Graduate Institute of Brain and Mind Sciences, College of Medicine, National 
Taiwan University, Taipei City, Taiwan.
(4)Department of Psychology, National Taiwan University, Taipei City, Taiwan.

OBJECTIVES: Previous literature using the mini-ultimatum game (the mini-UG) 
suggests that older adults consider outcomes more than others' intentions during 
fairness-related decision-making, whereas younger adults show the opposite 
pattern. Age-related declines in theory of mind (ToM) and executive functioning 
(EF) have been suggested as potential mechanisms underlying these age-related 
differences, but specific mechanisms remain unclear. The present work examines 
whether and how neural and behavioral factors known to be related to ToM and EF 
are associated with age-related differences in fairness processing.
METHOD: Thirty-six younger (Mage = 21.19, SDage = 3.14) and 36 older (Mage = 
72.08, SDage = 5.87) participants completed both magnetic resonance imaging 
(MRI) anatomical brain scans and the mini-UG alongside behavioral measures of 
ToM and EF outside of the scanner. Volumes and cortical thickness of ToM- and 
EF-related brain regions were extracted. Computational modeling of participant 
mini-UG decisions estimated individuals' tendencies to consider intention vs. 
outcome information.
RESULTS: Older adults relied more on outcomes than intention information, 
whereas younger adults showed the opposite pattern. Structural brain indices and 
behavioral measures did not mediate age-related differences in decision-making. 
However, dmPFC volumes moderated the age differences in decision-making, and EF, 
but not ToM, was positively associated with intention-based (vs. outcome-based) 
decisions across age groups.
DISCUSSION: These findings extend prior work on age differences in 
intention-based vs. outcome-based fairness consideration by showing that dmPFC 
volume may be one factor contributing to age differences in related decisions.
